Dose-dependent effects of micro-aeration on methane production and 
lignocellulose degradation during continuous anaerobic digestion of 
food waste
Ziyu Xiong a,1, Yutong Wu a,1, Jinglin Li b, Yafan Cai c, Xingyao Meng a,*, Pan Wang a,  
Lianhai Ren a
a School of Light Industry Science and Engineering, Beijing Technology and Business University, Beijing, 100048, China
b China IPPR International Engineering Co, Ltd., Beijing, 100089, China
c School of Chemical Engineering, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou, 450001, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Bioenergy
Micro-aeration
Waste valorization
Methane recovery
Microbial functional potential
A B S T R A C T
While micro-aeration is a promising strategy to enhance hydrolysis and acidogenesis in anaerobic digestion (AD), 
its dose-dependent effects on lignocellulose degradation and methane production under different total solids (TS) 
conditions remain unclear. This study investigated continuous AD of food waste (FW) at TS levels of 6% and 10% 
under oxygen loading rates of 0, 2.625, 5.25, and 10.50 mLO2/LR/d. At TS = 6%, 2.625 mLO2/LR/d modestly 
increased methane yield from 527.2 to 561.9 mL/gVSadded and increased cellulose removal to 60.16%. At 5.25 
mLO2/LR/d, biogas production increased further, whereas methane content decreased, indicating enhanced 
upstream substrate conversion rather than proportionally enhanced methanogenesis. At TS = 10%, improved 
methane production was observed only at 2.625 mLO2/LR/d, while higher oxygen loading impaired process 
performance. Excessive aeration caused volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation, increased oxidation reduction 
potential (ORP), and reduced lignocellulose degradation. Microbial community analysis showed oxygen- 
dependent shifts in lignocellulose-associated bacteria and methanogens, while PICRUSt2-based prediction sug­
gested changes in hydrolysis-related functions, energy metabolism, and oxidative-stress-response potential. 
Overall, the effective oxygen-loading window narrowed with increasing TS, and low oxygen input modestly 
improved methane production, whereas moderate oxygen loading mainly enhanced upstream substrate 
conversion.
1. Introduction
FW management has become a critical issue in sustainable waste 
treatment, resource recovery, and greenhouse gas mitigation. In 2022, 
approximately 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted globally, 
contributing an estimated 8–10% of global greenhouse gas emissions [1,
2]. Anaerobic digestion is widely recognized as an effective technology 
for FW treatment because it enables organic stabilization, methane re­
covery, and nutrient recycling [3,4]. However, FW contains lignocellu­
losic fractions such as vegetable stalks and fruit peels, in which cellulose, 
hemicellulose, and lignin are embedded in a recalcitrant matrix that 
limits enzymatic accessibility and hydrolysis efficiency [5,6]. As hy­
drolysis is generally regarded as the rate-limiting step in FW AD, 
improving lignocellulose solubilization while maintaining stable meth­
anogenesis is essential for enhancing the overall conversion of FW into 
methane.
Several studies have explored ways to improve the performance of 
AD, including substrate pretreatments, optimizing process parameters 
and introducing additives. However, the pretreatment or supplementary 
additives usually required extra energy and chemicals, thereby 
increasing operational costs and process complexity and potentially 
causing environmental concerns. Recent studies have shown that micro- 
aeration, which involves injecting small amounts of air or oxygen into an 
anaerobic system, has attracted increasing attention as a cost-effective 
strategy for improving digestion performance by accelerating hydroly­
sis and acidogenesis and providing more available substrates for

methanogenesis [7–11]. Recent studies have also highlighted the po­
tential of micro-aeration in continuous FW AD, while indicating that 
solids content, viscosity, and reactor stability may influence its effec­
tiveness [12]. Moderate oxygen exposure can stimulate hydrolytic and 
facultative microorganisms to secrete higher levels of extracellular en­
zymes (e.g., cellulases and xylanases). This enzymatic enhancement 
accelerates the disruption and degradation of complex lignocellulose, 
thereby providing more readily available substrates for methanogenesis. 
In FW AD, micro-aeration has been shown to affect hydrolysis, VFA 
dynamics, methane production, and microbial community structure [13,
14]. Moreover, appropriate oxygen loading can enhance methane pro­
duction and lignocellulose degradation, whereas excessive aeration may 
impair methanogenesis despite promoting organic matter removal [15,
16]. However, the interaction between TS content and oxygen loading in 
continuous food-waste anaerobic digestion remains insufficiently un­
derstood. 
These 
findings 
indicate 
that 
the 
effectiveness 
of 
micro-aeration depends strongly on oxygen dosage, substrate properties, 
and reactor operating conditions.
The effects of micro-aeration are inherently dose dependent. 
Appropriate oxygen input can be rapidly consumed by facultative mi­
croorganisms, creating localized redox gradients that favor hydrolysis 
and acidogenesis while preserving anaerobic niches for methanogenesis. 
In contrast, excessive oxygen may inhibit strictly anaerobic metha­
nogens, promote oxidative mineralization of organic carbon, and lead to 
VFA accumulation or methane-yield reduction [17,18]. Therefore, the 
central challenge is to define an appropriate oxygen-loading window 
that enhances hydrolysis without disrupting downstream methano­
genesis. This challenge is particularly relevant in continuous FW AD, 
where accelerated hydrolysis may increase soluble organic matter and 
VFA formation, whereas methanogenesis may respond more slowly, 
leading to decoupling between hydrolysis and methanogenesis kinetics. 
Although previous studies have shown that micro-aeration can regulate 
substrate hydrolysis, VFA production, methane generation, and micro­
bial communities, its effects depend strongly on oxygen input and 
reactor 
operating conditions [19,20]. Whether 
the favorable 
oxygen-input range becomes narrower as reactor loading increases, and 
how this is associated with the balance between upstream substrate 
conversion and downstream methanogenesis, remains insufficiently 
characterized. Because TS and OLR covary in many practical high-solids 
digestion systems, understanding their combined operational context is 
important for defining oxygen-input strategies without over-attributing 
the observed response to either factor alone. Therefore, a better un­
derstanding of the TS-dependent response to micro-aeration is needed to 
identify an appropriate oxygen-loading window while avoiding adverse 
effects on methanogenesis.
In this study, continuous AD of FW was conducted under two TS 
levels (6% and 10%) with different micro-aeration loading rates. The 
objectives were to (i) characterize the responses of continuous FW AD to 
increasing oxygen loading at 6% and 10% TS levels; (ii) assess their 
effects on methane production, process stability, VFA dynamics, SCOD, 
and lignocellulose degradation; and (iii) develop a proposed interpre­
tation of the process responses through microbial community and pre­
dicted functional analyses. Attention was given to the balance between 
enhanced upstream substrate conversion and maintenance of down­
stream methanogenesis under different oxygen-loading conditions. This 
study characterizes the responses under two TS conditions at a similar 
nominal organic loading rate (OLR) and provides a basis for selecting 
oxygen inputs to enhance lignocellulose conversion and methane re­
covery while maintaining stable methanogenesis.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
To ensure consistency in the experiment, the FW substrates were 
prepared in the ratio of cabbage: celery: tofu: meat: rice= 2:2:1:1:2. 
Before further use, FW was chopped. The main characteristics of FW 
used were as follows: TS of 13.33% ± 0.84, volatile solids (VS) of 
95.22% ± 1.21 (based on TS), soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) 
of 30550 ± 125.00 mg/L, pH of 7.63 ± 0.12. Sludge from AD of domestic 
waste served as inoculum and was taken from the Beijing Dongcun 
comprehensive treatment plant. The main characteristics are as follows: 
TS of 7.51% ± 0.96, VS of 53.50% ± 0.84 (based on TS), SCOD of 
8715 ± 54.37 mg/L, pH of 8.46 ± 0.10.
2.2. Continuous methane production from food waste via micro-aerobic- 
enhanced anaerobic digestion
2.2.1. Reactor configuration and operating parameters
Continuous AD experiments were conducted in double-jacketed glass 
reactors with a total volume of 5 L and a working volume of 4 L, 
maintained at 37 ± 1 ◦C. The daily feeding and withdrawal volume were 
140 and 84 mL for the TS = 6% and TS = 10% systems, corresponding to 
a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 28.6 d and 47.6d, respectively. The 
reactors were fed once daily, with an OLR of approximately 2.00 g VS/L/ 
d for both the TS = 6% and 10% systems. Each reactor was mechanically 
stirred at 20 rpm and equipped with a top feed port and biogas outlet 
and a bottom effluent outlet. After achieving stable anaerobic operation, 
the reactors were maintained for an additional 5-day stabilization period 
for this experiment, and operational stability was defined as relatively 
stable daily gas production for 3 consecutive days.
2.2.2. Selection of TS levels and oxygen-loading rates
Based on preliminary batch experiments, TS levels of 6% and 10% 
were selected and designated as R1 and R2, respectively. These levels 
represent different solids-loading conditions. These two TS levels were 
used to represent different solids-content conditions while maintaining a 
similar nominal OLR of approximately 2.00 g VS/L/d. The 6% TS system 
was expected to have greater fluidity and more favorable mass transfer, 
whereas the 10% TS system was expected to have lower fluidity and 
greater sensitivity to oxygen-input fluctuations. Four consecutive 
oxygen-loading phases were established at 0, 2.625, 5.25, and 10.5 
mLO2/LR/d. The oxygen-loading rates were selected based on previous 
studies and preliminary experiments to cover low, intermediate, and 
relatively high oxygen inputs. The anaerobic phase was designated CK, 
while the three micro-aeration phases were designated T1, T2, and T3, 
respectively. For each TS condition, two parallel reactors were operated 
continuously for 60 d, with each oxygen-loading phase maintained for 
15 d. The corresponding operational phases were designated R1_1–R1_4 
and R2_1–R2_4 for the TS = 6% and 10% systems, respectively.
2.2.3. Aeration delivery
Air was supplied directly into the digestate using a peristaltic pump 
(BT100–2J/YZ) at 0.5 mL air/min. Oxygen loading = air flow rate ×
aeration duration × 0.21/working volume. Aeration was conducted four 
times per day at 6 h intervals, with each aeration event lasting 25, 50, 
and 100 min for T1, T2, and T3, respectively, corresponding to total 
daily aeration durations of 100, 200, and 400 min/d. The produced 
biogas was collected in 10-L aluminum foil gas sampling bags (45 cm ×
35 cm; Changde BKM Biological Technology Co., Ltd.).
2.2.4. Sampling schedule
pH and ORP were monitored daily. Liquid samples were collected 
every 3 d for SCOD, TCOD, and VFA analyses. Microbial community 
samples were collected once during the late, operationally stable period 
at the end of each 15-d operational phase.
2.3. Analysis methods
TS, VS, ammonia nitrogen (NH4
+-N) and SCOD were measured by 
standard methods [21]. pH and ORP were measured with a portable pH 
meter (SX620, Shanghai) and portable ORP meter (SX630, Shanghai).

The volume of biogas production was tracked using the water 
displacement method. The methane content and VFA were determined 
by a gas chromatograph (GC-2014C, Shimadzu, Japan).
2.4. Microbial analysis
Microbial community samples were collected once during the late, 
operationally stable period at the end of each 15-d operational phase. 
2 mL of digestion broth was centrifuged (15,000 rpm, 10 min) and the 
sediment used for microbial community analysis. Genomic DNA was 
extracted with the PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit and verified by 1% 
agarose gel electrophoresis. The bacterial 16S rRNA V3–V4 and archaeal 
V4–V5 regions were PCR-amplified using 515FmodF and 806RmodR 
primers, respectively, quantified with the QuantiFluor™-ST system, and 
sequenced on Illumina MiSeq (Majorbio) after TruSeq™ library con­
struction. Functional profiles and the relative abundance of predicted 
enzyme-related genes were inferred using PICRUSt2. (http://huttenh 
ower.sph.harvard.edu/galaxy).
2.5. Statistical analysis
Pearson correlation analysis was performed to evaluate the re­
lationships among physicochemical parameters, AD performance, 
lignocellulose degradation, and process efficiencies. Correlation co­
efficients (Pearson’s r) range from −1 to 1, with positive and negative 
values indicating positive and negative correlations, respectively. Sta­
tistical significance was determined at P < 0.05. Mantel tests based on 
Bray–Curtis dissimilarity were used to evaluate the associations between 
bacterial or archaeal community composition and environmental and 
process variables.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. The effect of micro-aeration conditions on methane production of 
food waste
Fig. 1 investigates the effects of varying oxygen loads on gas pro­
duction in continuous AD reactors treating FW at TS levels of 6% and 
10%. At TS = 6%, both biogas and methane yields increased at oxygen 
loads of 2.625 and 5.25 mLO2/LR/d. The methane yields reached 561.9 
and 560.2 mL/gVSadded, respectively, compared with 527.2 mL/gVSad­
ded under anaerobic conditions. However, further increasing the oxygen 
load to 10.50 mLO2/LR/d resulted in a marked decrease in methane 
yield to 382.3 mL/gVSadded, corresponding to a 27.49% decrease rela­
tive to the anaerobic condition.
At TS= 10%, an improvement in methane production was observed 
only at an oxygen load of 2.625 mLO2/LR/d, where the methane yield 
increased to 648.7 mL/gVSadded, compared with 530.3 mL/gVSadded 
under anaerobic conditions. In contrast, methane yields decreased to 
524.9 and 391.0 mL/gVSadded at oxygen loads of 5.25 and 10.50 mLO2/

moted methane production, whereas excessive oxygen loading inhibited 
methanogenic performance. A similar decrease in biogas yield with 
increasing oxygen loading has also been reported in previous studies 
[13]. This inhibitory effect may be attributed to the poor fluidity and 
mass-transfer characteristics of high-solids systems, as well as the 
destabilization of anaerobic microbial communities under excessive 
oxygen exposure. Overall, the effects of micro-aeration on methane yield 
were strongly dose dependent, with improvement observed primarily 
under low oxygen loading. However, excessive oxygen significantly 
inhibited reactor performance by reducing overall biogas production 
and

3.2. The tendency of physicochemical properties during anaerobic 
digestion of food waste in micro-aerobic conditions
3.2.1. Variations of pH, ORP, NH4
+-N, and SCOD during continuous 
digestion
Fig. 2 (A-D) illustrates the effects of varying oxygen loading rates on 
pH, ORP, NH4
+-N, and SCOD during the anaerobic digestion of FW at 
different TS levels (6% and 10%).
ORP measurements showed changes in bulk redox conditions with 
oxygen input (Fig. 2B). At TS= 6%, ORP ranged from −374 to −346 mV 
during CK, from −368 to −351 mV at 2.625 mLO2/LR/d, and from −367 
to −343 mV at 5.25 mLO2/LR/d. These overlapping ranges indicate that 
the lower oxygen inputs did not produce a clearly separated bulk redox 
regime. At 10.50 mLO2/LR/d, ORP increased to −328 mV by the end of 
the phase, while pH decreased to 7.07. At TS = 10%, ORP ranged from 
−378 to −369 mV during CK and from −373 to −341 mV at 2.625 
mLO2/LR/d. Under the higher oxygen-loading conditions, greater fluc­
tuations and an eventual increase toward approximately −332 mV were 
reported. The pH of the TS = 10% system remained within 7.32–7.68 
over the experiment. Interpreted together with VFA profiles and 
methane production, the redox changes are consistent with a shift in the 
balance between upstream substrate conversion and downstream 
methane formation. The different responses may reflect the combined 
effects of solids content, OLR, and mass-transfer conditions. However, 
ORP integrates multiple redox processes and is influenced by pH; it does 
not quantify dissolved oxygen (DO) or establish spatial oxygen distri­
butions. The treatments are therefore defined by nominal oxygen input, 
with ORP providing complementary evidence of the bulk redox 
response.
As depicted in Fig. 2(C), NH4
+-N concentration remained at a rela­
tively low level at TS = 6%. During the oxygenation phase of 2.625–5.25 
mLO2/LR/d, the NH4
+-N concentration showed minor fluctuations and 
remained relatively stable. This indicated that micro-aerobic conditions 
moderately promoted the hydrolysis and ammonification of nitrogen- 
containing macromolecules, and the release rate achieved a dynamic 
balance with microbial assimilation and methanogenic consumption. In 
the high-oxygen stage, the NH4
+-N concentration exhibited substantial 
oscillations with a declining trend. This could be attributed to the 
elevated oxygen levels stimulating the activity of aerobic or facultative 
microorganisms, which accelerated the consumption of certain nitrogen 
sources or induced localized partial nitrification.
In TS= 10% system, the overall NH4
+-N level increased significantly 
due to the higher substrate concentration. During the micro-aerobic 
stage, the introduction of trace oxygen accelerated the hydrolysis and 
release of nitrogenous organic matter, resulting in a steady upward trend 
in NH4
+-N concentration. Under the medium-oxygen condition, mass 
transfer was limited by the high solid content, causing intense localized 
hydrolysis and acidogenesis. Consequently, the NH4
+-N release rate 
notably exceeded the microbial assimilation rate, leading to a distinct 
NH4
+-N peak in the system. During the 10.5 mLO2/LR/d stage, the NH4
+-N 
concentration initially experienced a sharp decrease followed by a 
substantial increase. The temporary decline was likely due to the 
depletion of readily degradable nitrogenous substrates. The subsequent 
increase could be attributed to the intense micro-aerobic conditions 
further disrupting the structure of residual refractory proteins, thereby 
triggering deep hydrolysis, coupled with the cell death and autolysis of 
inhibited microorganisms. Furthermore, the variation pattern of NH4
+-N 
concentration was consistent with the accumulation trend of SCOD, 
which further verified the potential risk of methanogenic inhibition in 
high-solid systems during the high-oxygen stage.
As shown in Fig. 2(D), in TS= 6% system, oxygen loads of 
2.625–5.25 mLO2/LR/d accelerated substrate hydrolysis, supplying 
ample small-molecule substrates for methanogens. The slight inhibition 
of methanogens under these conditions was offset by the increased 
substrate availability, leading to a slow SCOD accumulation. 
Conversely, under high oxygen conditions (TS=10%), severe methano­
genic inhibition blocked Soluble Organic Matter (SOM) degradation, 
resulting in a significant and continuous rise in SCOD. In TS= 10% 
system, SCOD remained relatively stable during the micro-aeration 
phase, indicating a temporary metabolic balance between substrate 
hydrolysis and methanogenesis. This led to massive accumulation of 
SOM, a sharp increase in SCOD, and a decline in methanogenic effi­
ciency. At 10.5 mLO2/LR/d, the observed decrease in SCOD was mainly 
attributed to localized oxidative decomposition of soluble organics 
rather than methanogenic degradation [22]. These variations in SCOD 
are consistent with the findings regarding methanogenic efficiency 
discussed above. This may reflect an imbalance between substrate sol­
ubilization 
and 
downstream 
consumption 
under 
the 
higher 
oxygen-input condition.
3.2.2. Characteristics of VFA production and lignocellulose degradation 
during continuous digestion
Fig. 2 (E-H) demonstrates that the regulation of solids content played 
a significant role, with the efficacy of micro-aeration exhibiting a non- 
linear relationship with oxygen concentration, consistent with previ­
ous studies [9,23,24]. Total VFA (TVFA) concentrations in both R1 and 
R2 initially decreased before increasing.
In R1, TVFA levels dropped to a maximum of 1531.96 mg/L and an 
average of 1307.29 mg/L, remaining stable with no accumulation. 
However, high oxygen levels led to TVFA accumulation and the inhi­
bition of methanogens, resulting in a decreased methane yield. In R2, 
TVFA decreased under the micro-aeration treatment, indicating that 
metabolic equilibrium was achieved [25]. Although TVFA remained 
stable at moderate oxygen levels, the synergistic inhibition of metha­
nogens by high oxygen and high NH4
+-N, combined with the effects of 
reactive oxygen species (ROS), reduced methanogenic efficiency. Acetic 
acid remained the predominant component of VFA in both systems, a 
characteristic unaltered by micro-aeration [26]. Under low and mod­
erate oxygen conditions, acetic acid was consumed efficiently, and 
propionic acid was maintained at extremely low concentrations, sug­
gesting that oxygen facilitated the conversion of propionate to methane 
[27].
At TS = 10%, degradation improved during phases R2_2 and R2_3; 
however, under the highest oxygen loading (10.50 mLO2/LR/d), the 
apparent removal values of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin became 
negative. These negative values indicate an apparent enrichment of the 
corresponding lignocellulosic fractions in the residual solids relative to 
the anaerobic baseline, rather than net formation of these components. 
Similar dose-dependent responses have been reported in lignocellulose- 
based anaerobic digestion, where moderate micro-aeration enhanced 
cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, whereas further increases in 
oxygen loading reduced methane production and disrupted the micro­
bial community structure [14]. Moderate micro-aeration can stimulate 
lignocellulose-degrading 
microorganisms 
and 
enzymes, 
thereby 
improving the hydrolysis of cellulose and hemicellulose; however, 
excessive oxygen exposure may impose oxidative stress on obligate 
anaerobes, particularly methanogens, and consequently disturb the

Under such conditions, the further conversion of recalcitrant lignocel­

in the TS= 10% system, suggesting a narrower oxygen-tolerance range

in Section 3.1.
3.2.3. Analysis of hydrolysis, acidification, acetogenesis, and 
methanogenesis efficiencies during continuous digestion
Fig. 3. reveals distinct response patterns of process efficiencies to 
oxygen loads in the two systems, indicating that the regulatory effect of 
micro-aeration was closely correlated with solids content.
In the R1 system, hydrolysis efficiency under micro-aeration 
improved by 19.49%, 17.31%, and 28.15% compared to the anaerobic 
phase, which is consistent with the SCOD generation profile. Acidifica­
tion efficiency initially decreased and then increased with rising oxygen 
loads, mirroring the trend observed in TVFA concentrations. Aceto­
genesis efficiency improved by 11.62% only at 5.25 mLO2/LR/d, align­
ing with the increased acetate content during this phase. The calculated 
methanogenesis efficiency increased at 2.625 and 5.25 mLO2/LR/d; 
however, the response of methane content differed between these two 
conditions. At 5.25 mLO2/LR/d, the increase in total biogas production 
was accompanied by a decrease in methane content, indicating that the 
enhanced overall gas production was primarily driven by intensified 
upstream substrate conversion rather than a proportional enhancement 
of methanogenesis. At 10.50 mLO2/LR/d, methanogenesis efficiency 
declined by 27.50%, consistent with the deterioration in methane 
production.
The efficiency variations in R2 differed from those in R1. Improve­
ments in hydrolysis, acidification, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis 
efficiencies were achieved simultaneously only at 2.625 mLO2/LR/d, 
exceeding the anaerobic phase by 6.22%, 6.13%, 9.81%, and 16.23%, 
respectively. Conversely, at 10.50 mLO2/LR/d, all efficiencies dropped 
significantly by 24.69%, 36.53%, 35.50%, and 33.21% compared to the 
anaerobic phase, suggesting that the digestion stability of high-solids 
systems is more susceptible to the adverse effects of oxygen.
Integrating the efficiencies of the four conversion steps, it is recom­
mended to control the micro-aeration dosage at 2.625–5.25 mLO2/LR/ 
d for low-solids FW AD. For high-solids systems, the dosage should not 
exceed 2.625 mLO2/LR/d. This conclusion aligns with the observed 
patterns of methanogenic efficiency.
The increase in methane production under appropriate micro- 
aeration may be attributed to the improved coordination between hy­
drolysis and methanogenesis [18]. Limited oxygen input promoted 
substrate solubilization and hydrolysis while avoiding substantial VFA 
accumulation, thereby increasing the availability of soluble in­
termediates for subsequent methanogenesis [13]. This interpretation is 
supported by the simultaneous improvement in hydrolysis and meth­
anogenesis 
efficiencies 
under 
the 
appropriate 
oxygen-loading 
conditions.
3.3. Microbial community analysis
3.3.1. Microbial community composition at phylum and genus levels during 
continuous digestion
Fig. 4 (B-E) illustrates the characteristics of the microbial community 
at the phylum and genus levels in continuous anaerobic digestion of FW 
enhanced by micro-aeration.
At the bacterial phylum level, Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, Actino­
bacteriota, and Synergistota were the predominant phyla in both the R1 
and R2 systems, accounting for a total relative abundance of 85.53%- 
96.85%. Their functional complementarity supported the digestion 
process. In the R1 system, the abundance of Firmicutes, the core acid­
ogens, showed a decreasing trend with increasing oxygen concentration. 
However, the uniform mass transfer inherent to the low-solids envi­
ronment ensured a basal abundance sufficient to maintain hydrolysis 
and acidification functions. The enrichment trend of Bacteroidota (which 
enhances substrate hydrolysis) aligned with the variations in SCOD 
generation and hydrolysis efficiency. Actinobacteriota has been reported 
to participate in lignocellulose degradation [29], while Synergistota is 
known to mediate the conversion of propionate to acetate. Although the 
total bacterial abundance was high during the high-oxygen phase, 
facultative anaerobes became enriched, and their aerobic metabolism 
competed for metabolic substrates with methanogens. This disrupted the 
metabolic balance, resulting in enhanced hydrolysis and acidification 
but inhibited methanogenesis. In the R2 system, changes in community 
composition were highly consistent with methanogenic efficiency 
trends. In phases R2_1 and R2_3, the abundance of Firmicutes was 
similar, and functional groups like Bacteroidota showed no significant 
enrichment, corresponding to unchanged methanogenic efficiency. Only 
in R2_2 did Firmicutes remain stable while Bacteroidota showed slight

At the genus level, community shifts were consistent with the 
phylum-level patterns. Streptococcus, a dominant facultative genus 
within Firmicutes, remained stable under low oxygen but declined 
under high oxygen in the low-solids system, potentially weakening

pobium, supporting hydrolysis and VFA conversion. For archaea, 
Nanoarchaeota-related taxa were enriched at low-to-medium oxygen 
under TS= 6%, whereas Methanobacteriaceae/Methanobacterium in 
TS= 10% responded positively only to low oxygen, mainly via hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis. Medium and high oxygen inhibited 
methanogenic genera, confirming the broader oxygen tolerance of the 
low-solids system.
3.3.2. Correlation analysis
Mantel test analysis revealed a significant positive correlation be­
tween TS and SCOD (Fig. 4A). This is attributed to the increased 
degradation and digestion of organic matter available in high-solids 
systems. Conversely, TS showed a significant negative correlation with 
acidification and acetogenesis efficiencies. This was likely due to the 
lower mass transfer efficiency inherent in high-solids AD, which hin­
dered substrate diffusion and inhibited the growth activity of acidogenic 
and acetogenic bacteria.
Oxygen exhibited a positive correlation with SCOD, TVFA, acetate, 
and cellulose removal, indicating that oxygen introduction facilitated 
organic matter degradation and TVFA generation. A significant negative 
correlation was observed between pH and both TVFA and acetate, 
confirming that the decline in system pH was driven by the substantial 
accumulation of VFA, particularly acetate. Biogas yield and cumulative 
methane yield (CMY) were significantly positively correlated with 
methanogenic efficiency and lignin removal rates, highlighting the 
critical role of lignocellulose degradation in methane production. 
Furthermore, significant positive correlations were found among the 
efficiencies of hydrolysis, acidification, acetogenesis, and methano­
genesis, as well as with cellulose and hemicellulose removal rates, 
suggesting the four digestion steps were tightly interlinked.
Regarding the relationships between microorganisms and environ­
mental factors, both bacteria and archaea showed significant positive 
correlations with SCOD, indicating their joint participation in substrate 
degradation. Oxygen was positively correlated with bacteria but nega­
tively correlated with archaea. It is hypothesized moderate oxygen 
levels enhanced substrate hydrolysis by stimulating bacterial activity, 
while the produced intermediate metabolites could be further utilized 
by methanogens under anaerobic microenvironments. Conversely, 
archaea were negatively correlated with TVFA and positively correlated 
with methanogenic efficiency, reflecting their role in consuming organic 
acids to enhance methane production. Furthermore, bacterial commu­
nities were closely associated with hemicellulose and lignin removal, 
while archaeal communities showed stronger correlations with cellulose 
and hemicellulose degradation.

KEGG pathway analysis were conducted. These analyses provide pre­

activities or metabolic processes. The potential effects of micro-aeration

3.5. Proposed interpretation for methane production in micro-aeration 
enhanced anaerobic digestion of food waste
Based on the integrated analyses of reactor performance, physico­
chemical characteristics, microbial succession, enzyme prediction, and 
KEGG pathways, the response to micro-aeration was governed by a 
balance between accelerated upstream substrate conversion and pres­
ervation of downstream methanogenic capacity ( Fig. 6). Appropriate 
oxygen input altered the abundance of functional microorganisms such 
as Firmicutes and increased the predicted abundance of hydrolysis- 
related functions, including α-glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.20), thereby accel­
erating lignocellulose decomposition and soluble substrate release [45]. 
In the TS = 6% system, the observed response may be associated with 
more favorable mass-transfer conditions, which could allow moderate 
oxygen input to promote upstream substrate conversion without severe 
inhibition of methanogenesis. In contrast, higher TS= 10% system 
showed a narrower apparent favorable response to oxygen loading. This 
greater sensitivity may be associated with the higher solids content, 
altered rheological and mass-transfer characteristics, and greater spatial 
heterogeneity under the TS = 10% condition. Microbial community 
shifts and PICRUSt2-derived functional predictions were generally 
consistent with this process-level interpretation, which showed a higher 
predicted abundance of TCA-cycle-related functions and improved 
oxidative-stress tolerance. However, excessive oxygen disrupted this 
balance, leading to oxidative stress, VFA accumulation, and methano­
genic inhibition. Overall, the beneficial effect of micro-aeration depen­
ded on matching oxygen dosage with solids content, enabling 
simultaneous enhancement of substrate degradation and methane pro­
duction. It should be noted that the functional profiles obtained from 
PICRUSt2 represent predictions based on 16S rRNA gene data rather 
than direct measurements of gene expression, enzyme activity, or 
metabolic flux. Therefore, the predicted functional changes should be 
interpreted as potential metabolic associations. In this study, these 
predictions were interpreted together with the experimentally measured 
process performance, VFA profiles, lignocellulose degradation, and mi­
crobial community data to provide a mechanistic hypothesis rather than 
definitive evidence of pathway activation. Overall, the present results 
support a conceptual framework in which the benefit of micro-aeration 
depends on maintaining a balance between oxygen-stimulated upstream 
carbon conversion and oxygen-sensitive downstream methanogenesis. 
Direct validation using metagenomic/metatranscriptomic analyses and 
targeted enzyme or metabolite measurements would be valuable in 
future studies.
3.6. Preliminary energy assessment
A preliminary energy balance was assessed from the experimental 
data. The energy input was calculated from the operating voltage of the 
peristaltic pump (10 V) and the recorded average current (15 mA). For 
the calculated daily aeration durations of 100, 200, and 400 min, the 
corresponding pump electricity inputs are 0.25, 0.50, and 1.00 Wh/d, 
respectively. These estimates apply to both TS conditions and assume 
that the stated voltage and current represent the actual electrical input 
during aeration; they exclude standby, mixing, heating, and other 
auxiliary electricity. They should therefore be interpreted as conditional 
estimates rather than measured total reactor energy consumption. At TS 
= 6%, the net energy gains relative to the anaerobic control were 
approximately 2.34 and 1.99 Wh/d at oxygen loading rates of 2.625 and 
5.25 mLO2/LR/d, respectively, whereas a net energy loss of 12.66 Wh/ 
d was observed at 10.5 mLO2/LR/d. At TS = 10%, the lowest oxygen 
loading rate provided the greatest net energy gain of approximately 
9.22 Wh/d, while higher oxygen loading rates resulted in negligible or 
negative energetic benefits.
Therefore, the present calculation should be regarded as a 
preliminary estimate of the additional electricity requirement for air 
delivery rather than a complete energy or economic assessment. The 
results suggest that controlled micro-aeration may provide a favorable 
energy balance under the tested conditions, although pilot- and full- 
scale studies are still necessary to assess oxygen transfer, mixing, total 
energy consumption, and long-term stability with precisely controlled 
dosing [46].
4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that the effectiveness of micro-aeration on 
continuous FW AD was strongly dependent on oxygen loading and TS 
content. Low oxygen loading of 2.625 mLO2/LR/d resulted in a modest 
improvement in methane production and process stability in both TS 
systems, while the TS = 6% system tolerated a wider oxygen range of 
2.625–5.25 mLO2/LR/d. Under appropriate micro-aeration, lignocellu­
lose degradation was promoted, with cellulose removal reaching 
60.16% and lignin removal increasing by up to 26.10%. In contrast, 
excessive aeration at 10.50 mLO2/LR/d adversely affected process sta­
bility, as indicated by increased ORP, VFA accumulation, pH decline, 
SCOD fluctuation, reduced methane production, and weakened ligno­
cellulose degradation. The TS= 10% system showed lower oxygen 
tolerance, likely due to restricted mass transfer and greater spatial het­
erogeneity. Microbial community and predicted functional analyses 
suggested that appropriate oxygen input favored hydrolysis-related 
bacteria, methanogens, and increased the predicted potential for hy­
drolysis, electron transfer, and oxidative-stress response. Overall, the 
findings highlight the importance of matching oxygen input with reactor 
loading conditions to maintain coordination between upstream sub­
strate conversion and downstream methane formation. Micro-aeration 
exerted distinct effects on hydrolysis and methanogenesis: low oxygen 
loading could modestly improve methane production while maintaining 
methanogenic stability, whereas moderate oxygen loading primarily 
promoted upstream substrate conversion without a proportional in­
crease in methane formation.
